summary: An early specification of Domain Name System Security Extensions, adding digital signatures to DNS data so answers can be checked for authenticity. It incorporates feedback on RFC 2065 from early implementers and replaced that document. It was itself replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: This early DNSSEC specification adds signatures so a resolver can check DNS data and its source. It also defines records that prove when a name or record type does not exist.

questions: what is the dns sig record
what is the dns nxt record
subtitle: An early DNS security design using signed records, public keys and authenticated denial of existence.

tldr.problem: Ordinary DNS records do not prove their origin or integrity, so a resolver cannot verify that an answer is authentic or that a name is absent.
tldr.mechanism: DNSSEC in this RFC adds KEY records for public keys, SIG records for signatures and NXT records for signed proof that names or record types do not exist.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2535 replaced RFC 2065 and was later obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

today: RFC 2535 was obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. It had replaced RFC 2065.

sections.title: Services and Limits of the Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 2535 extends the Domain Name System (DNS) with public-key distribution, authentication and integrity for DNS data, and optional authentication of DNS transactions and requests. It incorporates feedback from early implementers of RFC 2065.

The design treats DNS data as public. It does not provide query or response confidentiality, access-control lists or denial-of-service protection. The extensions aim to let security-aware resolvers verify records using trusted keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions help resolvers check whether DNS data is authentic and unchanged. They do not hide DNS queries or stop denial-of-service attacks.

sections.title: KEY Records and Zone Trust
sections.content:
A KEY resource record (type 25) associates a public key with a DNS name, such as a zone, host or user. The record carries flags, a protocol value, an algorithm value and key material. A signed KEY record can also assert that a zone has no key.

A resolver begins with one or more trusted public keys. It can trust additional zone keys only when they are signed by keys that its policy accepts. RFC 2535 names DSA as mandatory to implement and RSA/MD5 as recommended for its specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A KEY record associates a public key with a DNS name. A resolver trusts a new zone key only when it can follow a valid signature back to a key it already trusts.

sections.title: SIG Records and Signed DNS Data
sections.content:
A SIG resource record (type 24) signs a resource-record set and identifies the signer and the period when the signature is valid. Its fields include the covered type, algorithm, original TTL, signature inception and expiration, key tag, signer name and signature.

Signatures use a canonical form of the records, including the original TTL, so changes made by caches do not invalidate verification. A special SIG with type covered set to zero can sign a DNS response together with the query that produced it. That transaction signature does not itself authenticate individual records.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIG record identifies who signed a set of DNS records and the period when the signature is valid. A resolver checks the signature against a trusted key before accepting the records as authenticated.

sections.title: NXT Records Prove What Is Missing
sections.content:
SIG records authenticate data that exists, but do not prove that a name or type is absent. An NXT resource record (type 30) gives the next existing name in canonical order and a bitmap of record types at its owner name. Together, NXT records form a chain through the names in a zone.

For a missing name, a security-aware server returns an NXT record covering the name and its signature. For a missing type, the bitmap shows the type is absent. The RFC notes that walking the complete chain can reveal every name in a zone, even if zone transfers are prohibited.
sections.plainLanguage: An NXT record names the next existing name and lists the record types at its own name. A resolver can use the signed chain to verify that a requested name or type is absent.

sections.title: Following a Chain of Trusted Signatures
sections.content:
A resolver starts with a statically configured trusted key and follows alternating SIG and KEY records until it reaches the data being checked. Resolver policy determines which signer may authenticate which name, and the validity periods of signatures in the chain constrain the result.

The AD bit in a response says that the server authenticated the answer and authority data according to its policy. The CD bit in a query says pending, unauthenticated data is acceptable. A resolver MUST NOT trust AD unless it trusts the server and has a secure path to it or uses transaction security.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver can follow signatures from a key it already trusts to the key that signed an answer. The AD flag is useful only when the resolver also trusts the server and its connection.

sections.title: Conformance and Security Boundaries
sections.content:
The RFC defines BASIC and FULL conformance levels for servers and resolvers. A basic server can store and retrieve SIG, KEY and NXT records; a full server also creates signatures, includes security records in responses and handles the AD and CD bits. Primary servers for secure zones MUST be fully compliant.

DNSSEC can establish the validity of records retrieved from DNS, but does not prevent an attacker from replacing a host at the resulting address or capturing traffic to it. The RFC also says secure time synchronization is needed because signatures have validity periods.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC can verify DNS records, but it cannot protect every part of a connection to the address those records contain. Systems also need trustworthy time to check signature dates.
